# Orion 3, by the numbers

## Cold open
A new model shipped on Tuesday with no warning. No keynote, no countdown, no teaser trailer. Just a changelog entry and a price page. Within a day, every developer forum was arguing about the same three numbers. By Friday, two rivals had cut their prices. This is the story of those numbers, and what they do and do not prove.

## The benchmark everyone quoted
Start with the headline score. On Terminal-Bench, Orion 3 scored 57.6%. The model before it, Orion 2, scored 41.2%. That is a jump of more than sixteen points in a single release. The closest rival, Vega 5, sits at 52.1%. On paper, Orion 3 leads by five and a half points, and that is the number every headline used. Look closer at that 57.6% though. It was measured at high effort, with a long thinking budget that most teams will never pay for. At medium effort, the same model scores 49.8%, which puts it below Vega. The bars look the same until you read the footnote under the chart. Orion 2 at 41.2% was measured at medium effort too. Compare like with like and the jump is closer to eight points than sixteen. Eight points is still a real gain, and still the largest this year from any lab. The leaderboard has never moved this much in one release. Either way, the headline number is the best case, not the typical one, and the gap to Vega is two points at most.

## The price page
Now the price. Orion 3 costs $2 per million input tokens and $8 per million output tokens. Vega 5 charges $3 and $15. On output, which is where agents spend most of their money, Orion is almost half the price. Picture a hundred agent runs on the same task. Sixty two of them finish under a dollar on Orion. Only thirty eight finish under a dollar on Vega. That gap is the whole sales pitch, and it is printed in bold on the price page. Cached input drops to $0.20 per million, a tenth of the list price. For a coding agent that rereads the same repository all day, that cached rate matters more than anything else on the page. Most teams will never see the list price at all. Their bills will be mostly cached reads and output tokens, the two lines where Orion is cheapest. So the price story is real, it compounds over a month of use, and it is bigger than the benchmark story.

## What developers found
The first week of real use told a different story again. Developers ran Orion 3 on their own repositories and posted the results, with the pull requests linked. The most shared thread compared it against Vega 5 on forty real pull requests from open source projects. Orion fixed 31 of them. Vega fixed 27. That is closer than the benchmark suggests, four pull requests out of forty. Speed was the surprise. Orion answered in 1.8 seconds on average, against 4.6 seconds for Vega. Faster answers mean shorter loops, and shorter loops mean more attempts in the same hour. A developer who waits less tries more, and trying more is how hard bugs get fixed. That is the advantage developers kept mentioning in the thread, more than the score. So the lead is speed and price first, and quality a distant third.

## What it means
Put it all together. A model that is a little better, a lot cheaper and much faster. Rivals answered within a week. Vega cut its output price to $10. A third lab, Lyra, announced a model priced at $6. The price war is the real launch. Watch the next round of prices, not the next benchmark.
